I've seen some mention of the rubidium and caesium atomic clocks 
being used for time standards on the GPS constellation.  While it's
true that these clocks are used for generating the system time for 
the GPS, it's not actually the clocks on the satellites that provide
the time.  Instead, each satellite uses a set of clocks to keep 
track of time locally, but this time is compared to the GPS system 
time via an uplink every 4 hours.  The GPS system time is 
maintained by the GPS control segment at Schriever AFB in Colorado, 
and is generated by a set of atomic clocks located at that facility. 
The rubidium and caesium clocks on the satellites are therefore used 
in conjunction with the GPS system time, but aren't actually the 
system clocks themselves. 

The same is true for GLONASS and the other NAVSTAR-like 
constellations: the system time is maintained centrally and the 
satellite-borne clocks keep local time which is periodically 
updated via uplink.

The Mir space station's daily orbit does indeed shift due to the Earth's
slightly ellipitical shape, however this has nothing to do with its
de-orbiting.  The decay of an object's orbit is primarily due to
atmospheric drag.  Mir is outside of the atmosphere, in a regime known
as the 'exosphere', but this is still not a perfect vacuum and there are
molecules which provide sufficient drag to have an effect on the
spacecraft's orbit over time (months and years).  The Earth's slightly
elliptical shape does affect the orbit of a body like Mir, but this
effect is not all that significant over the lifetime of Mir.
